- `mise run check` — fast inner loop (format check, clippy, unit tests).

- `mise run snap` — run the snapshot-bearing engine and wire tests and

- `mise run dev` — blessed bring-up: Postgres, fresh worktree database,

Every rule here and in the files above exists because it is non-obvious,

fell into; they are not a route description, and satisfying them is not
the same as thinking.

Prefer a smaller number of larger, coherent PRs over many small ones. A new

threshold moves, or additions unrelated to the work at hand — get their own
dedicated PR. Never weaken a rule to get a branch green.

Everything durable in the repo — docs, code comments, exemplar entries,
error messages, READMEs — reads standalone, to a reader with no access to
any plan, decision register, or task tracker: state the thing itself, in
plain language. Planning shorthand (decision numbers, unit or task
labels, plan-section references) lives only in PR bodies and commit
messages, where git keeps the history.

A test that verifies the wrong thing is a live risk to this codebase, not
an asset to preserve.

- The sin is **silent weakening**: loosening an assertion, deleting a

  without saying so. This applies equally to invariant checks, lints,
  fixtures, and thresholds.
- Regression corpora are append-only.
- Never assume a failure is pre-existing — check against the merge base
  with main before claiming it.

Agents are authors by default; these surfaces need a human in the loop.
Say so in the PR and wait for explicit human review when a change touches:

- invariant documentation;

# AGENTS.md

Working agreement for anyone — agent or human — changing this repository.
This file is an index of non-inferable facts: exact commands, banned
surfaces, where the invariants live, and what "done" means. Depth lives in
`docs/agent-guides/`; architecture lives in `ARCHITECTURE.md`. Read those
on demand; never inline their content here.

## Commands

First time on a machine: `mise trust && mise install` — nothing else, except
the 1Password CLI (`op`) for `mise run secrets`, which you install yourself.

- `mise run check` — fast inner loop (format check, clippy, unit tests).
  Not a gate; nothing merges on this.
- `mise run sweep` — trim this worktree's build cache to its 8 GiB
  budget, oldest generations first. `check` runs it.
- `mise run pre-pr` — THE merge gate. CI runs exactly this task, so local
  green is CI green. Run it before every PR.
- `mise run test` — full suite via nextest plus doctests; refuses pending
  snapshots.
- `mise run snap` — run the snapshot-bearing engine and wire tests and
  auto-accept their changes.
- `mise run fmt` — format. Uses the pinned nightly rustfmt; never run bare
  `cargo fmt`.
- `mise run dev` — blessed bring-up: Postgres, fresh worktree database,
  both binaries.
- `mise run db` — recreate this worktree's database from nothing.

## Definition of done

- `mise run pre-pr` is green on your branch — actually run, output in
  hand. A claimed run must have really happened; paste the command and
  result in the PR.
- Snapshot changes are regenerated deliberately (`mise run snap`) and
  committed; no `.snap.new` files anywhere.
- The PR template is filled in, including the novelty lane (below).

## Banned surfaces

Reasons and replacements print at the violation site; this is the map of
where the rules live, not a restatement of them:

- `clippy.toml` — workspace-wide disallowed calls: wall clock, ambient
  randomness, environment reads, print macros.
- `crates/structure-tests/tests/ban_table.rs` — greppable house bans
  (thread sleep, and rows added as habits are mined) whose replacement
  text is the error message.
- `crates/structure-tests/tests/` — the shape rules: declared crate
  characteristics agree with the workspace dependency graph; the engine
  fold's dependency graph declares all four importability characteristics
  (`docs/characteristics.md`); test machinery is never reachable from a
  production dependency graph.
- Boundary code that genuinely needs a banned call takes a scoped `#[allow]`
  with a comment at the call site.

## Rules are traps, not maps

Every rule here and in the files above exists because it is non-obvious,
was hit repeatedly, and is actionable. Rules mark holes people actually
fell into; they are not a route description, and satisfying them is not
the same as thinking.

Prefer a smaller number of larger, coherent PRs over many small ones. A new
rule that directly pins an invariant established by a slice belongs in that
slice when the PR argues for it explicitly. Other rule changes — removals,
threshold moves, or additions unrelated to the work at hand — get their own
dedicated PR. Never weaken a rule to get a branch green.

## Durable artifacts are evergreen

Everything durable in the repo — docs, code comments, exemplar entries,
error messages, READMEs — reads standalone, to a reader with no access to
any plan, decision register, or task tracker: state the thing itself, in
plain language. Planning shorthand (decision numbers, unit or task
labels, plan-section references) lives only in PR bodies and commit
messages, where git keeps the history.

## Tests are never a golden baseline

A test that verifies the wrong thing is a live risk to this codebase, not
an asset to preserve.

- If you believe a test is wrong, act on that belief **openly**: fix or
  delete it, with the reason stated in the PR description. That is
  legitimate and encouraged.
- The sin is **silent weakening**: loosening an assertion, deleting a
  case, skipping a test, or regenerating a snapshot only to reach green,
  without saying so. This applies equally to invariant checks, lints,
  fixtures, and thresholds.
- Regression corpora are append-only.
- Never assume a failure is pre-existing — check against the merge base
  with main before claiming it.

## Human fences

Agents are authors by default; these surfaces need a human in the loop.
Say so in the PR and wait for explicit human review when a change touches:

- the event-contract enums — the closed set of inputs the core accepts;
- invariant documentation;
- safety-critical surfaces: anything that moves money, sequences inputs,
  or defines the durable log formats.

## The novelty lane

Novelty is never forbidden — it is made impossible to miss.

- The PR template asks which existing pattern you followed (link it; the
  catalog is `docs/agent-guides/exemplars.md`) or why none fit. "None
  fit" requires a short design note in the PR body.
- CI comments on every PR that adds a crate, dependency, public trait, or
  module, so the declaration is checked against the diff, not trusted.
- Rust APIs are deliberately unstable before v1; the compatibility gate
  returns when the workspace begins publishing stable versions.

## Pointers

- `ARCHITECTURE.md` — what the system is and where things live.
- `docs/characteristics.md` — what makes a crate importable by the fold.
- `docs/agent-guides/exemplars.md` — the "to add X, copy Y" catalog.
- `crates/services/README.md` and `migrations/README.md` — the rules of
  the two grouped areas.

- intent=ack → do not respond

Use `hcom <cmd+flags> --name {instance_name}` for every hcom command:

## AGENTS (fleet lifecycle)

Provision and cull Claude/Codex peer sessions through `$AI_CONFIG_ROOT/tools/fleet`. hcom owns identity and messages; herdr owns pane/worktree placement. herder is the fleet's display cache, registrar and observer; it never masters identity (hcom) or placement (herdr), and no lifecycle verb consults herder's store before acting. `herder list` joins the live views with the store's provenance for display only; `herder register` records lifecycle facts and performs none.

With no placement flag, the wrapper opens a new tab in your current herdr workspace; use sibling panes (`--split-from`) only when the operator directs it. When `--group` is absent, an agent launcher passes its own current group to the new seat; a human launch inherits nothing, and `--group ''` explicitly suppresses inheritance. The wrapper writes group/title after hcom returns the new name and before it records `launch-ready`. Titles are short kebab-case and never repeat the seat's name (it is shown beside the title). Every seat commits as the checkout's own git identity: the pane launch pins `GIT_AUTHOR_*`/`GIT_COMMITTER_*` from `git config user.name`/`user.email` resolved at the pane cwd, which outranks any `git -c user.email=…` a seat passes. - Message: `hcom send @name --intent request --thread THREAD --name {instance_name} -- 'message'`
- Compact a worker: check `hcom list <name> status`; when ordering matters also inspect `hcom term <name> --json`; then `hcom term inject <name> '/compact <steer>' --enter` and send one continuation with `hcom send`. Queued delivery is success; never resend.

- Fork: create a verified idle pane, then `FLEET_PANE=<pane> HCOM_TERMINAL=fleet hcom f <name-or-uuid>`.
